newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO to try to tempt Moscow with revamped package.
newsitem.headline: NATO to try to tempt Moscow with revamped package.

text.p: NATO has revamped a package of measures offering Russia an upgraded relationship with the West designed to lessen its opposition to the alliance's plans to expand into eastern Europe, alliance sources said on Friday.

The package, which has at its centrepiece the offer of some form of permanent consultative forum between the two former foes, will be presented to Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Monday by alliance Secretary-General Javier Solana.

Solana, who has been mandated by alliance countries to negotiate a new charter or treaty with Moscow, is now hoping to break the impasse with Russia over enlargement well before a July summit at which the new members will be named.
That summit in Madrid is due to endorse enlargement, a radical overhaul of the alliance's command structures and a formal new partnership with Russia.

"These are the three key vectors of NATO's transformation. Up to now, they have been developing in parallel. Our aim is to make them converge by the time of the summit in July," Solana said during a visit to Austria on Thursday.
But NATO sources say time is running out and Solana will seek to flatter the Russians into serious talks by stressing a new deal with Moscow is now the alliance's number one priority.
NATO officials say the package contains no new thinking, but ideas for more flexibility on arms control, greater military cooperation, and more economic aid have been fleshed out.

"It is more a question of presentation and timetable, the idea is to convey the message that NATO is attaching more importance to its relations with Russia than anything else," said one senior official.

The package was endorsed by the European allies during a tour of Brussels, Paris, Bonn and London this week by Strobe Talbott, Deputy U.S. Secretary of State and Washington's point man on relations with Russia.
NATO diplomats say the Russians, aware that enlargement will go ahead one way or the other, could be tempted by the idea of the deal being clinched at a separate summit before July.
"That would allow (President Boris) Yeltsin to present himself as the man who can do real business with the West with which it is now on a par," said one military source.

Solana, who is due to have five hours of talks with Primakov at an official guest house near Moscow, sees the task of negotiating the new deal as the major challenge of his tenure of the post of secretary-general.
NATO insiders are playing down expectations of what might emerge from the encounter, but admit Solana will be disappointed if he does not at least win a commitment for a second meeting.
"No one is anticipating changes in either position at this stage, but Solana wants to get the ball rolling," said an alliance diplomat.

Solana, an experienced negotiator who as Spanish foreign minister clinched several key European Union deals, must convince the Russians he is the man who speaks for the West and with whom they can do business.
Diplomats say that will not be an easy task.
Virtually the entire political class in Russia baulk at the prospect of some the former Soviet Union's satellites as members of the military alliance that won the Cold War.
Alliance diplomats say Russian diplomacy is currently focused on limiting expansion to as few countries as possible and delaying it as long as possible.
"The Russians will try and prevaricate as much as possible, and exploit any differences within the alliance by separate approaches to the Americans, the Germans, and so on," added the diplomat.

Solana will try and tempt Moscow into real dialogue with offers of more flexibility on arms control issues, such as changes to the landmark Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) accord, and more economic assistance.
But the main plank is the offer of a permanent mechanism for consultation on issues ranging from nuclear proliferation, terrorism, anti-missile defence systems, and international crime.
It could take the form of a standing committee and be enshrined in a charter or treaty.
"Virtually everything could be covered, but neither side could veto the other's plans," said one official.

NATO has already said it would not station nuclear weapons on the territory of the first new members, widely-expected to be Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, and hinted it would make the same commitment for conventional forces.
